source.title: SPICE: Simple Polysemantic Feature Interpretation via Clustering-based Explanation
source.authors: Sehyun Lee; Dahee Kwon; D. Lee; Jaesik Choi

page_placements.theme: Feature pathways, circuit decomposition and compositional reuse

record.file_problem: The paper and supplementary material are present; some figure text is garbled, but the pathway-overlap results used here are stated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures attribution-pathway overlap for two polysemantic neurons and reports different pathway patterns for related versus unrelated concepts. It does not use or test the toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The study examines polysemanticity in vision models, but does not test sparse-feature superposition, feature capacity, dedicated dimensions, or one-dimensional feature geometry. The separability tables compare the authors' clustering method with baselines and do not measure those claim objects. The study's cited discussion of superposition and SAE work is not its own result.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. SPICE clusters attribution footprints to split polysemantic neurons in vision models. It takes polysemanticity as given and cites superposition as one cause, but tests no capacity, sparsity or geometry account. The pathway-overlap case studies (18% vs 42%) describe how two neurons' concepts are wired upstream. They do not compare capacity pressure with other causes, so they bear on no version, including V3. The other evaluations score SPICE against baselines.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is that SPICE is a simple, architecture-general, scalable way to disentangle polysemantic neurons without a preset K. Using it, the authors also report that CNNs and ViTs differ in polysemanticity across depth. They further report that polysemantic neurons form through diverse pathways, from overlapping to largely disjoint circuits.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses attribution clustering and pathway-overlap analysis in pretrained vision architectures; it does not reproduce toy-model feature-vector training or measure superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pathway-overlap comparison varies with whether the concepts are related or unrelated.

fits_no_version.finding: Upstream attribution-pathway overlap differs between two ViT-B block-11 polysemantic neurons: 18% for unrelated concepts (#13) and 42% for related concepts (#371).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemantic neurons that encode related concepts share upstream circuits more than those that encode unrelated concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: SPICE concept-cluster counts and attribution-similarity distributions vary by architecture and depth. ViT shows late-layer multimodality (43% of block-11 neurons significant on the Dip Test); ResNet-50 stays unimodal. ViT yields more clusters per neuron than ResNet-50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron-level polysemanticity in vision models differs systematically between CNNs and Transformers and across depth.

record.peer_reviewed: European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV 2026), as stated
record.problems: The pathway evidence is based on two reported neuron examples, without a stated control or uncertainty estimate for the overlap values. The study does not compare pathway mechanisms against capacity pressure or test causal explanations for polysemanticity.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were extracted as rows: the clustering-separability and runtime evaluations measure the proposed method, not the claim versions' capacity or superposition objects; cited results are excluded.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, no feature/dimension or sparsity sweep, no geometry.
All of it: no test of capacity competition or of importance deciding dedicated vs shared dimensions.
All of it: no test separating capacity-driven polysemanticity from other causes. The pathway case studies do not address this.
All of it: only vision models are studied; no LLMs or SAE features.
All of it: SAEs are only cited.
All of it: feature dimensionality is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V3 'supports' label is removed. The pathway overlap for two neurons, with no control, does not test whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure, and the record itself says so in its untested parts. The study states polysemanticity arises 'from data statistics and superposition constraints', citing the original and Marshall & Kirchner, but does not test this. The separability, CoSy, threshold and runtime results are method evaluations and were rightly not extracted as rows.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparse-feature or dimension sweep, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition is tested.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity, or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The pathway analyses indicate heterogeneous circuit patterns, but do not establish that these arise independently of capacity pressure or show that polysemanticity is not evidence of superposition.
No LLMs or SAE-recovered features are studied.
No claim about SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical units is tested.
The study does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional features.

relation.reason: Section 2 cites superposition constraints as an explanation for polysemanticity. SPICE itself uses attribution clustering, without relying on or testing the listed superposition claims.

tranche.reason: SPICE analyzes neuron polysemanticity and attribution pathways, a related construct. It neither tests any listed superposition version nor uses superposition as a tool; the related-work citation does not establish T4.

source_check.notes: The pathway overlaps describe two selected neurons; they do not establish whether capacity pressure causes their polysemanticity. No verdict on the listed claim versions is warranted.
